Dad fell asleep on the couch during the film he insisted we all watch. We covered him with a blanket and kept watching, quiet, so he would not miss the ending he will swear he saw.
Grandma tastes the soup, adds salt, and says it needs more love. When she is not looking, my little brother adds a pinch of salt too, and whispers, 'There. Now it has both.'
My son lost his first tooth and left it under his pillow with a note: 'Dear Tooth Fairy, please leave the money and take the tooth. Do not wake me up. I am sleeping.' Dad still has the note.
My daughter drew our family for school. The dog is bigger than Dad, Mum has a crown, and I am standing on the roof, because, she explained, 'that's where you fix things.'
Every Sunday we argue over the last roast potato. Last week Grandad ate it while we were still arguing, then said grace for it, very solemnly, like it was a small hero.
I taught my daughter to drive. She parallel-parked perfectly on the first try, then looked at me and said, 'Relax, Dad. You taught me.' I have never been prouder, or quieter.
Our dog waits by the front door every day at 5:58, two minutes before the school bus turns the corner. He has never once been wrong, and he has never once been thanked out loud.
My little brother hid in the laundry basket to surprise Mum. He fell asleep in it, and she found him folded in among the towels, snoring, holding a sign that said 'BOO!' in crayon.
For Mum's birthday the kids made breakfast in bed. They set off the smoke alarm twice and presented the burnt toast like a trophy. She ate every bite and asked for the recipe.
Grandad turns his hearing aid off during arguments and on again for the grandkids' stories. Last week he heard the whole of a story about a frog, twice, and asked for it again.
